ai.text:
The European Parliament has approved a change to an EU rule on the key information document, the short paper that explains packaged investment and insurance-based investment products to ordinary buyers. The vote was 311 in favour and 261 against, with 38 abstentions. The change aims to keep this document short and easy to read by cutting out anything that is not essential or is repeated.

Under the change, the document must stand on its own and be clearly separate from marketing material. It should not point to marketing material or contain investment recommendations. It may refer to other documents, such as a prospectus where relevant, but only for information that belongs in the key information document itself. If a product offers a range of investment options that cannot fit in one short document, the document should still give at least a general description of those options and the product's costs apart from the costs of the investment options.

Product makers must give investors tools that help them research and compare the different investment options. Where technically possible, these tools should show the total cost of the product, including the cost of the insurance cover, as well as risks and performance, and they should link to the detailed pre-contract information for the underlying investments. Investors must also be told the total cost before they are bound by any contract or offer, and this is also met if the information is provided electronically.

The electronic and paper versions must have identical content. Consumers can ask for a paper copy, which must be provided free of charge. The European supervisory authorities must make the document streamlined, standardised and user-friendly, with simple cost information, and where useful, tables and graphs. The information must be limited to what is strictly necessary, and performance information must be comparable across different types of products.

The document will also include the sustainability profile of these products, since investors increasingly want that information. By 31 December 2030, the Commission must report on whether an EU-wide comparison tool for these products is feasible, assessing its impact, costs and benefits. If appropriate, the report will be accompanied by a legislative proposal. The European Parliament, the Council and the Commission have said that investors should have easy access to reliable, independent information to compare options across the EU.

summary.label: Legislative Observatory, Decision by Parliament, 1st reading
summary.text:
The European Parliament adopted by 311 votes to 261, with 38 abstentions, a legislative resolution on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014 as regards the modernisation of the key information document.
The European Parliament adopted its position at first reading by amending the Commission's proposal as follows:
Form and content of the key information document
The key information document is meant to be a concise document. To achieve that goal, a three-page limit was set in Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014. This regulation requires new elements to be included in the key information document. At the same time, the key information document should remain clear and easy to read . That entails streamlining its content and presentation in such a way as to avoid any non-essential or redundant information.
The amended text clarifies that the key information document should be a standalone document, clearly separate from marketing communications . It should not contain cross-references to marketing communications or any investment recommendations. It may contain cross-references to other documents, including a prospectus where applicable, provided that those cross-references relate to information that is to be included in the key information document under this Regulation.
Where a packaged retail and insurance-based investment product offers a retail investor a range of investment options that cannot be provided within a single, concise standalone document, the key information document should provide at least a generic description of the underlying investment options and information on the costs of the product other than the costs for the investment option.
The packaged retail and insurance-based investment product manufacturers should:
(a) provide retail investors with tools, adapted to those investors, that facilitate research and comparison among the different investment options offered , including on the costs of the underlying investment options and, where technically feasible, on: (i) the total cost of the product, including the costs relating to the investment options and those relating to the insurance cover; and (ii) the risks and performance. These tools should contain a link to the pre-contractual information documentation relating to the investment products backing the underlying investment options;
(b) inform retail investors of the total cost of the product , including the costs relating to the investment options and those relating to the insurance cover, in good time before those investors are bound by any contract or offer to invest in a given investment option. This condition should also be deemed to be fulfilled when retail investors are informed of the total cost of the product, including the costs relating to the investment options and those relating to the insurance cover, in electronic format.
Care must be taken to ensure that the content of the key information document is identical in both electronic and paper formats , guaranteeing that both formats provide access to all relevant information contained within the document. Consumers may request a paper copy of the key information document. This paper version should be provided free of charge.
Where appropriate in order to provide fair, clear and not misleading information to retail investors, different approaches may be taken for different types of products.
In addition, when developing draft regulatory technical standards, the ESAs should ensure that key information documents present essential information in a streamlined, standardised and user-friendly format that allows for comparability , including simplified cost disclosure and, where relevant, tables and graphs to improve clarity. The simplified cost disclosure should include a user-friendly presentation of the total cost borne by the retail investor and a breakdown of that cost.
To allow the retail investor to easily understand the key information document, the European supervisory authorities should also ensure that the information provided in that document is limited to what is strictly necessary .
When developing the draft regulatory technical standards, the European supervisory authorities should ensure that appropriate performance information is comparable across different types of packaged retail and insurance-based investment products.
Sustainability profile
Retail investors are increasingly seeking information on the sustainability performance of investment products, including packaged retail and insurance-based investment products. Therefore, it is important to include the sustainability profile of packaged retail and insurance-based investment products in the key information document.
Comparison tool
No later than 31 December 2030, and following the incorporation of key information documents into the European Single Access Point (ESAP), the Commission should prepare a report on the introduction of a comparison tool for packaged retail and insurance-based investment products at EU level. This report should contain a feasibility study for such a comparison tool, including an assessment of its impact, costs, and benefits.
Where appropriate, the report will be accompanied by a legislative proposal relating to a Union-wide comparability tool for all packaged retail and insurance-based investment products or for a subset of packaged retail and insurance-based investment products.
The European Parliament, the Council and the Commission have stated in this regard that retail investors should have easy access to reliable and independent sources of information, so that they can make informed investment decisions based on a comprehensive comparison of the different investment options available in the Union.
